The steam has far more heat to give than the ice needs, so the mixture settles at
**100 °C** with some steam left uncondensed.
**Step 1 — find the heat the ice needs to reach 100 °C.**
melting: mL_f = 1 x **80 = 80 cal** ✓
heating 0 → 100 °C: mcΔT = 1 x 1 x 100 = **100 cal** ✓
total needed = **180 cal** ✓
**Step 2 — find the heat 1 g of steam can give on condensing.**
mL_v = 1 x **540 = 540 cal** ✓
**Step 3 — compare.** 540 > 180 ✓ so the steam **more than suffices**. Not all of it
need condense, and the temperature cannot fall below 100 °C.
**Step 4 — find how much steam actually condenses.**
m = 180/540 = **⅓ g** ✓
**Step 5 — state the final state.** 100 °C, with **1⅓ g of water** and **⅔ g of steam**
coexisting ✓
**Temperature = 100 °C** ✓
**Why the answer is not somewhere in between.** The latent heat of steam, **540 cal
g⁻¹**, is enormous - nearly seven times the latent heat of fusion, and more than five
times the heat needed to raise water from 0 to 100 °C ✓ A gram of steam is a far larger
energy store than a gram of ice is an energy sink.
**The check by energy balance.**
given out: ⅓ x 540 = **180 cal** ✓
taken in: 80 + 100 = **180 cal** ✓ balanced exactly, with the temperature pinned at the
boiling point throughout.
**Why a phase change holds the temperature constant.** The energy goes into **breaking
intermolecular bonds**, not into raising the molecules' kinetic energy ✓ so the
thermometer does not move until the change is complete.
**Why steam burns are so much worse than boiling-water burns.** A gram of steam at
100 °C delivers **540 cal** on condensing, and only then begins to cool ✓ A gram of
water at 100 °C cooling to body temperature gives about 63 cal. Steam is nearly nine
times as damaging.
**How to spot the answer quickly.** Compare the **total available** heat with the
**total required** ✓ If the giver has more than enough, the final temperature is the
giver's phase-change temperature. If the taker needs more, it is the taker's.
**The reverse question.** With 1 g of ice and only **0·3 g** of steam, the steam could
supply just 162 cal - short of 180 ✓ The ice would melt but the mixture would settle
**below** 100 °C.
**The values worth memorising.**
L_fusion of ice = **80 cal g⁻¹** ✓
L_vaporisation of water = **540 cal g⁻¹** ✓
specific heat of water = **1 cal g⁻¹ °C⁻¹** ✓
**Reading the distractors.** **0 °C** ✗ would need the ice to dominate - it cannot, with
a third of the heat capacity. **50 °C** ✗ and **55 °C** ✗ are naive averages, ignoring
latent heat altogether ✓
∴ 100 °C.

Use **λ = 12·27/√V Å** - or λ = h/√(2mK) in full.
**Step 1 — use the standard electron formula.** For a kinetic energy of V electron-volts,
λ = **12·27/√V Å** ✓
**Step 2 — substitute V = 120.**
λ = 12·27/√120
= 12·27/10·954 ✓
**Step 3 — evaluate.**
= **1·12 Å**
= 1·12 x 10⁻¹⁰ m
= **112 pm** ✓
**The check from first principles.**
K = 120 x 1·6 x 10⁻¹⁹ = **1·92 x 10⁻¹⁷ J** ✓
p = √(2mK) = √(2 x 9·11 x 10⁻³¹ x 1·92 x 10⁻¹⁷) = **5·91 x 10⁻²⁴ kg m s⁻¹** ✓
λ = h/p = 6·63 x 10⁻³⁴/5·91 x 10⁻²⁴ = **1·12 x 10⁻¹⁰ m** ✓ the same.
**Where the 12·27 comes from.**
λ = h/√(2m_e eV) ✓ and substituting the constants gives
λ = **1·227 x 10⁻⁹/√V m** = 12·27/√V Å. Worth memorising; it turns these questions into
one square root.
**Why this wavelength is interesting.** 112 pm is about an **atomic spacing** ✓ which is
why electrons of a hundred-odd volts diffract from crystals - the Davisson-Germer
experiment used 54 eV electrons, λ = 1·67 Å, and found a sharp Bragg maximum.
**The comparison with light.** A visible photon has λ ≈ **5000 Å** ✓ Electrons at this
modest energy have wavelengths **four thousand times shorter**, which is the whole basis
of electron microscopy's superior resolution.
**Why the energy must be raised so far for better resolution.** λ ∝ **1/√V** ✓ Halving
the wavelength needs **four times** the voltage, so high-resolution instruments run at
100-300 kV.
**The relativistic caveat.** At 120 eV, v/c = **0·022** ✓ so the non-relativistic formula
is accurate to about 0·02%. Above 50 keV the correction matters.
**The picometre.** 1 pm = 10⁻¹² m ✓ so 1·12 Å = 112 pm. Keeping the unit conversions
straight is half the battle in these problems.
**A sanity check on the speed.**
v = p/m = 5·91 x 10⁻²⁴/9·11 x 10⁻³¹ = **6·5 x 10⁶ m s⁻¹** ✓ fast, but comfortably
sub-relativistic.
**Reading the distractors.** **95 pm** ✗ corresponds to 167 eV; **102 pm** ✗ to 145 eV;
**124 pm** ✗ to 98 eV ✓ All are near misses, so the arithmetic must be done carefully -
√120 = 10·95, not 11.
∴ 112 pm.

At the closest approach **all** the kinetic energy has become electrostatic potential
energy.
**Step 1 — write the energy balance.** At the turning point the alpha particle is
momentarily at rest:
K = **(1/4πε₀)(2e)(Ze)/r₀** ✓
**Step 2 — rearrange.**
r₀ = **2kZe²/K** ✓
**Step 3 — substitute.** Gold has Z = **79**; K = 5 MeV = **8 x 10⁻¹³ J** ✓
r₀ = 2(9 x 10⁹)(79)(1·6 x 10⁻¹⁹)²/(8 x 10⁻¹³) ✓
**Step 4 — evaluate the numerator.**
2 x 9 x 10⁹ x 79 x 2·56 x 10⁻³⁸ = **3·64 x 10⁻²⁶** ✓
**Step 5 — divide.**
r₀ = 3·64 x 10⁻²⁶/8 x 10⁻¹³
= **4·55 x 10⁻¹⁴ m** ✓
**Step 6 — convert to centimetres.**
= 4·55 x 10⁻¹² cm ≈ **10⁻¹² cm** ✓
**Why 180° matters.** A head-on collision gives the **smallest** possible approach ✓ Any
other scattering angle leaves the particle with some transverse motion, so it never
comes so close. This is the limiting case.
**What Rutherford concluded from it.** The nucleus must be **smaller** than 4·55 x 10⁻¹⁴
m ✓ About 10⁻¹⁴ m against the atom's 10⁻¹⁰ m - a factor of ten thousand, which is why he
said it was "as incredible as if you had fired a fifteen-inch shell at a piece of tissue
paper and it came back and hit you".
**Why the atom is mostly empty.** The nucleus occupies about **10⁻¹²** of the atom's
volume ✓ so the overwhelming majority of alpha particles pass through almost
undeflected - as Geiger and Marsden found, with only about one in 8000 turning through
more than 90°.
**Why the alpha particle carries 2e.** It is a **helium nucleus**, two protons and two
neutrons ✓ hence the factor of 2 in the formula.
**Why this is only an upper limit on the nuclear size.** The alpha stops before touching ✓
At 5 MeV it is still outside the range of the **strong** force. Higher-energy probes get
closer, and the true radius of gold is about **7 x 10⁻¹⁵ m**.
**How nuclear radii are actually written.**
R = **R₀A^(1/3)** with R₀ = 1·2 fm ✓ For gold, A = 197: R = 1·2 x 5·82 = **7·0 fm** ✓
comfortably inside the 45·5 fm computed here.
**Why the result scales with Z.** r₀ ∝ **Z/K** ✓ A lighter target repels less and lets
the alpha closer; a more energetic alpha likewise. Both are used experimentally to probe
different depths.
**Reading the distractors.** **10⁻¹⁰ cm** ✗ is the atomic radius, a hundred times too
large. **10⁻¹⁴ cm** ✗ and **10⁻¹⁶ cm** ✗ are far smaller than any nucleus ✓
∴ 10⁻¹² cm.

The photon energy equals the **band gap**, so λ = hc/E_g.
**Step 1 — use the energy-wavelength relation.**
λ = **hc/E** ✓ and with hc = **1240 eV nm**,
λ(nm) = **1240/E(eV)** ✓
**Step 2 — substitute.**
λ = 1240/1·9 ✓
**Step 3 — evaluate.**
= **653 nm**
= **6·5 x 10⁻⁷ m** ✓
**What colour that is.** **Red** ✓ at the long-wavelength end of the visible spectrum -
which is exactly what a 1·9 eV LED looks like.
**Why the gap fixes the colour.** An electron in the conduction band recombines with a
hole in the valence band, and the energy released - **E_g** - leaves as **one photon** ✓
so the emission is narrow and nearly monochromatic. This is why an LED needs no colour
filter.
**The band gaps of common LEDs.**
GaAs **1·4 eV** → 885 nm, infrared ✓
GaAsP **1·9 eV** → 653 nm, red ✓
GaP **2·3 eV** → 540 nm, green ✓
GaN **2·8-3·4 eV** → blue and ultraviolet ✓
**Why blue LEDs took so long.** A wide-gap semiconductor that could be doped both ways
was needed ✓ **Nakamura, Akasaki and Amano** solved it with gallium nitride in the
early 1990s and shared the 2014 Nobel Prize. White LEDs - a blue LED with a yellow
phosphor - followed, and transformed lighting.
**Why an LED must be forward biased.** Forward bias drives electrons and holes **into**
the junction, where they recombine ✓ Reverse bias widens the depletion layer and sweeps
carriers apart, so no light is produced.
**Why silicon cannot make an LED.** Silicon has an **indirect** band gap ✓ Recombination
there requires a phonon as well as a photon, so the energy is released mostly as heat.
Direct-gap compounds such as GaAs are needed.
**Why LEDs are so efficient.** The energy of each recombination goes almost entirely
into **one** photon of the wanted colour ✓ An incandescent lamp wastes 95% as heat and
infrared; a good LED converts over half the electrical input to visible light.
**The turn-on voltage.** Roughly **E_g/e = 1·9 V** for this device ✓ which is why a red
LED lights at about 1·8-2 V and a blue one needs 3 V or more. The forward voltage is a
direct reading of the band gap.
**Why the emission is not perfectly sharp.** Thermal spread of order **kT ≈ 0·026 eV**
broadens it ✓ giving a line about 30 nm wide - narrow enough to look like a pure colour.
**Reading the distractors.** **2·9 x 10⁻⁹ m** ✗ is an X-ray wavelength, needing 430 eV.
**1·6 x 10⁻⁸ m** ✗ is extreme ultraviolet, and **9·1 x 10⁻⁵ m** ✗ far infrared ✓ Only
6·5 x 10⁻⁷ m is visible light, which an LED must emit.
∴ 6.5 × 10⁻⁷ m.

Total lift is **well depth + floor height**; power is the work divided by the time.
**Step 1 — find the total height raised.**
h = 25 + 35
= **60 m** ✓ from the water surface in the well to the first floor.
**Step 2 — find the mass.**
6 tonnes = **6000 kg** ✓
**Step 3 — find the work done.**
W = mgh = 6000 x 10 x 60 ✓
= **3·6 x 10⁶ J** ✓
**Step 4 — convert the time.**
20 minutes = **1200 s** ✓
**Step 5 — find the power.**
P = W/t = 3·6 x 10⁶/1200
= **3000 W = 3 kW** ✓
**Why the two heights add.** The water starts **25 m below** ground and finishes **35 m
above** it ✓ so it is raised through 60 m in all. Using only 35 m - forgetting the
well - is the error the question is built around, and gives 1·75 kW.
**Why the pump is rated higher in practice.** This is the **useful output** power ✓ A
real pump loses energy to friction in the pipes, turbulence, and electrical heating in
the motor. At 70% efficiency the electrical input would be 3/0·7 = **4·3 kW**.
**The energy in familiar units.**
3·6 x 10⁶ J = **1 kWh** ✓ - which is exactly 3 kW for 20 minutes, a pleasing check and a
reminder that the kilowatt-hour is just 3·6 MJ.
**What it would cost.** At about ₹7 per unit, **₹7** to lift six tonnes of water sixty
metres ✓ Raising water is cheap; it is the pumping of it at scale that adds up.
**Why the speed of lifting does not appear.** The water arrives with negligible kinetic
energy ✓ so all the work goes into **potential** energy. If it were discharged as a fast
jet, ½mv² would have to be added.
**The alternative route to power.**
P = **mgh/t** = (6000/1200) x 10 x 60 = 5 x 600 = **3000 W** ✓ working with the mass flow
rate, 5 kg s⁻¹, which is how pump specifications are usually written.
**Why g = 10 is specified.** To keep the arithmetic clean ✓ With g = 9·8 the answer is
2·94 kW - the same to two figures, and the option chosen is unaffected.
**A sense of scale.** 3 kW is about the power of an electric kettle ✓ Running for twenty
minutes it lifts six tonnes of water sixty metres - a vivid illustration of how much
work a modest power can do given time.
**Reading the distractors.** **6 kW** ✗ halves the time or doubles the mass. **1·5 kW** ✗
uses 30 m, and **12 kW** ✗ is four times too large ✓
∴ 3.

By equipartition, each of the three translational degrees of freedom carries **½kT**.
**Step 1 — state the equipartition theorem.** In thermal equilibrium, every **quadratic**
degree of freedom has average energy
**½kT** ✓
**Step 2 — count the degrees of freedom.** A molecule's translation has three - along
**x**, **y** and **z** ✓
**Step 3 — add them.**
E = 3 x ½kT
= **3/2 kT** ✓
**Why "ideal gas" means translation only.** An ideal gas is treated as **point**
particles with no internal structure and no intermolecular forces ✓ so the only energy
available is kinetic energy of translation.
**The connection to pressure.** From kinetic theory,
PV = ⅓Nmv̄² = ⅔N(½mv̄²) ✓
and with PV = NkT this gives ½mv̄² = **3/2 kT** directly ✓ - the same result derived
without invoking equipartition at all.
**Why temperature *is* molecular kinetic energy.** This equation defines it ✓
Temperature is not a separate thing that molecules possess; it is a measure of their
mean translational kinetic energy, and absolute zero is where that energy vanishes.
**The value at room temperature.**
E = 1·5 x 1·38 x 10⁻²³ x 300 = **6·2 x 10⁻²¹ J = 0·039 eV** ✓ the familiar "kT ≈ 1/40 eV"
of semiconductor physics.
**The r.m.s. speed that follows.**
v_rms = **√(3kT/m)** ✓ For nitrogen at 300 K, **517 m s⁻¹** - faster than sound, which is
no accident: sound travels by molecular collisions.
**Why real gases carry more.** A **diatomic** molecule can also rotate about two axes,
adding 2 x ½kT:
E = **5/2 kT** ✓ and at high temperature vibration adds a further kT, giving 7/2 kT.
This is why C_V differs between gases, and why it **rises in steps** with temperature -
a fact classical physics could not explain, and quantum mechanics could.
**For one mole.**
U = **3/2 RT** ✓ and C_V = 3/2 R = **12·5 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹** - measured accurately for helium
and argon, confirming the monatomic result.
**Why it is independent of the gas.** Neither the mass nor the chemical identity
appears ✓ Helium and xenon at the same temperature have the same mean energy per
molecule - the heavier simply moves more slowly.
**Reading the distractors.** **KT** ✗ counts two degrees of freedom - right for a
two-dimensional gas. **½kT** ✗ counts one, and **2KT** ✗ four ✓ Counting the
translational directions settles it.
∴ 3/2 KT.

Work done = **q(V_final − V_initial)**, with V the potential due to the other charge.
**Step 1 — note the separations.**
initially **5 cm = 0·05 m** ✓
finally **4 cm = 0·04 m** ✓
**Step 2 — write the potential energy at each separation.**
U = **kq_Aq_B/r** ✓
U_i = (9 x 10⁹)(3 x 10⁻⁹)(1 x 10⁻⁹)/0·05
= 2·7 x 10⁻⁸/0·05 = **5·4 x 10⁻⁷ J** ✓
U_f = 2·7 x 10⁻⁸/0·04 = **6·75 x 10⁻⁷ J** ✓
**Step 3 — find the work.**
W = U_f − U_i = 6·75 x 10⁻⁷ − 5·4 x 10⁻⁷ ✓
= **1·35 x 10⁻⁷ J** ✓
**The compact form.**
W = kq_Aq_B(1/r_f − 1/r_i)
= (9 x 10⁹)(3 x 10⁻¹⁸)(25 − 20)
= 2·7 x 10⁻⁸ x 5
= **1·35 x 10⁻⁷ J** ✓ noting that 1/0·04 = 25 and 1/0·05 = 20 m⁻¹.
**Why the work is positive.** Both charges are **positive**, so they repel ✓ Pushing
them closer requires work **against** the repulsion, and that work is stored as
potential energy. Letting them go, the system would return it as kinetic energy.
**Why only the two charges matter.** Potential energy is a property of the **pair** ✓
There is no "self-energy" term to worry about, and with only two charges there is a
single interaction.
**Why the 1/r dependence makes the last centimetre expensive.** The energy rises
**hyperbolically** as r falls ✓ Moving from 5 to 4 cm costs 1·35 x 10⁻⁷ J; from 2 to
1 cm would cost 1·35 x 10⁻⁶ J - ten times as much for the same one-centimetre step.
**The distinction between U and V.**
V = **kq/r**, a property of a point in space ✓
U = **qV**, the energy of a charge placed there ✓
Here V at 4 cm due to A is 675 V, and multiplying by 1 nC gives 6·75 x 10⁻⁷ J.
**Why the path does not matter.** The electrostatic force is **conservative** ✓ so the
work depends only on the initial and final separations, however the charge is moved.
**What would change for opposite charges.** U would be **negative**, and bringing them
closer would **release** energy ✓ The work done by an external agent would then be
negative - the charges do the work.
**A sanity check on the magnitude.** 1·35 x 10⁻⁷ J is minute ✓ as it must be for
nanocoulomb charges at centimetre separations - about the energy of a grain of sand
falling a hundredth of a millimetre.
**Reading the distractors.** **2·7 x 10⁻⁷ J** ✗ is twice the answer, as if the step were
to 1/0·033 m. **12·1 x 10⁻⁷ J** ✗ is U at 2·2 cm, and **2·0 x 10⁻⁷ J** ✗ matches no
step ✓
∴ 1.35 × 10⁻⁷J.
